report.source_text: Initially, 15 l of oxygen supplementation was administered through a non-rebreather mask, resulting in improved oxygen saturation to 86%, although cyanosis persisted. Given the consideration of respiratory and cardiac arrhythmic causes, the patient was administered a single intravenous dose of 100 mg hydrocortisone and a single infusion of 10% calcium gluconate in 100 ml normal saline over 10 minutes, respectively. Subsequently, a bolus of methylene blue (1 mg/kg over 10 minutes) and 20 ml/kg of colloid were administered.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 14-year-old Pakistani boy presented to the emergency department with acute onset (1.5 hours duration) of severe generalized headache, shortness of breath, generalized cyanosis involving the nose, lips, cheeks, trunk, limbs, and nail beds, and altered mental status (agitation, drowsiness, reduced responsiveness) following ingestion of one tablespoon of kalmi shora powder 2 hours prior for renal lithiasis. Physical examination revealed critical hypoxemia (SpO2 58%) with tachycardia (113 bpm), tachypnea (30/min), hypotension (100/60 mmHg), and hypothermia (34.5°C), with pronounced cyanosis of the trunk, chin, lips, oral mucosa, and nail beds. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated a pathognomonic saturation gap with normal partial pressure of oxygen (pO2 90 mmHg) but decreased oxygen saturation (SpO2 85%), accompanied by severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.02, lactate 20 mmol/L). Supplemental oxygen (15L via non-rebreather) improved SpO2 to 86% but cyanosis persisted, consistent with hemoglobin dysfunction rather than hypoxemic respiratory failure. The patient received methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV bolus, with rapid clinical response: within 10 minutes, oxygen saturation normalized to 100% on room air, consciousness was restored, and cyanosis significantly reduced, with complete resolution of bluish discoloration within 30 minutes. Subsequent chemical analysis of the ingested substance confirmed kalmi shora contained potassium nitrate.
